The Battle of Tours. In seven thirty-two, in central France, a Frankish army under Charles Martel faced an enormous Muslim Umayyad force led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi. The Muslim army was estimated at eighty to one hundred and twenty thousand strong, while Charles Martel commanded only thirty thousand. The battle lasted several days, a series of cavalry charges against Frankish infantry formations. Again and again, the Umayyad mounted forces attacked, and again and again, the Frankish soldiers held formation, repelling the charges.

Slowly the tide turned. The Muslim cavalry, for all their legendary prowess, could not break the disciplined Frankish infantry standing in close formation. The Umayyads were defeated and the northward expansion of Islamic forces was halted. Charles Martel earned his nickname—Charles the Hammer—through this victory, and it strengthened his political position enormously. He emerged as the undisputed military power in his region and set the stage for his family's rise to dominance.

The battle shaped the future of Europe itself. Western Europe would remain predominantly Christian rather than fall under Umayyad control. It marked a critical limit to Islamic territorial expansion and secured Christian hegemony in the West. So significant was this victory that Charles Martel's descendants would found the Carolingian dynasty, which would produce Charlemagne and reshape the entire medieval feudal system. A single battle in seven thirty-two echoed through centuries of history.
